The General. Buster Keaton's 1926 silent comedy set during the American Civil War, in which a railroad engineer pursues a stolen locomotive across enemy lines to reclaim both his train and his girlfriend. Keaton's deadpan genius and the film's precise timing and visual gags—all executed with dangerous practical stunts—make it a masterclass in silent physical comedy and one of the era's most entertaining films.

Directed by Buster Keaton and Clyde Bruckman, it was the most expensive comedy of the silent era at the time. Keaton's character, Johnnie Gray, pursues the locomotive General—a real eighteen-eighties engine—with stone-faced determination, never cracking a smile despite increasingly absurd situations. The train chase across Georgia is the film's centerpiece. Keaton performs dangerous stunts with meticulous choreography: riding on the engine, jumping between cars, with a real locomotive hitting a bridge.

Every gag is a miniature machine of precisely timed action, careful framing, and the locomotive's mechanics themselves becoming comedy. Smoke from the engine obscures Johnnie's vision. Water sprays his face. Visual puns and sight gags rely entirely on composition and timing. Dialogue cards are minimal, proving that comedy's structure transcends words.

The Civil War backdrop allows for satirical historical comedy. Johnnie's loyalty to his train supersedes ideology, and he ends up rescuing Southern soldiers—a deadpan subversion of war movie conventions. The General is often cited as Keaton's masterpiece and one of the greatest silent comedies ever made, rivaling Metropolis and Battleship Potemkin in technical achievement while remaining opposite in tone to contemporary Chaplin masterpieces equally beloved but more sentimental and introspective.
